video_title: Lawfare Daily: The Israeli Elections—What Does it All Mean?
gist: A Lawfare panel (Natan Sachs, Joel Braunold, Benjamin Wittes) unpacks Israel's October 27 election: Netanyahu's bloc fell from 68 to about 53 seats, the anti-Netanyahu Zionist parties hold about 48, and record Arab turnout gave the Arab parties about 19, leaving deadlock. They lay out unity-government, ultra-Orthodox realignment and repeat-election scenarios, Trump's push for unity without Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, and Netanyahu's warning that Israel faces banking sanctions.

insights.claim: Preliminary results of the October 27 Israeli election show roughly 53 seats for the pro-Netanyahu parties, 48 for the anti-Netanyahu Zionist parties and 19 for the two Arab-backed parties (Joint List and Ra'am), leaving no bloc at the 61-seat majority.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett (host)
insights.so_what: No coalition can form without someone breaking a campaign promise, making political paralysis the base case.
insights.quote: we don't have any party any coalition in the majority which needs 61 seats

insights.claim: Netanyahu's outgoing coalition went into the vote holding 68 of 120 Knesset seats (64 originally plus 4 from Gideon Sa'ar) and comes out with about 53-55, losing its governing mandate.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: The incumbent coalition lost roughly 13-15 seats despite the camp's public jubilation.

insights.claim: Likud is on track for about 27 seats versus about 22 for Gadi Eisenkot's party, so Netanyahu leads the largest party in the larger Jewish bloc while about 68 MKs belong to parties that will not recommend him.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: President Herzog faces conflicting precedents on who gets the first mandate.
insights.quote: If the current numbers hold, Likud will have 27 seats and Eisenlut will have 22.

insights.claim: Final results depend on uncounted 'double envelope' ballots, and the sizes of Yisrael Beiteinu and the ultra-Orthodox bloc could still shift and rescramble the coalition math.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Watch final certified counts before pricing any coalition outcome.

insights.claim: The formal timeline is official results on November 4, then 7 days for President Herzog to choose a candidate, who gets 28 days plus a possible 14-day extension to form a coalition; failure after two attempts plus 14 days triggers automatic new elections.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett (host) / Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Coalition uncertainty in Israel likely persists into December at minimum.

insights.claim: The main change versus four years ago is a surge in Arab-Israeli turnout to levels similar to Jewish turnout, adding roughly four seats to Arab parties, largely at the expense of ultra-Orthodox parties whose voters were depressed.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: If sustained, high Arab turnout structurally denies the religious right a standalone majority.

insights.claim: Benjamin Wittes argues the opposition effectively won about 68 seats and can form a government simply by accepting Arab parties' support, and that refusing to do so means the party system 'deserves another term of Netanyahu'.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: The outcome hinges on a political choice, not on arithmetic.
insights.quote: all you have to do is be willing to use them

insights.claim: Natan Sachs says relying on the Joint List would be unprecedented: unlike Ra'am, it would not formally join a coalition and its Balad component would struggle to vote for one, and in wartime many Israelis see dependence on it as a constraint on war decisions.
insights.speaker: Natan Sachs
insights.so_what: An Arab-backed minority government is morally possible but unlikely in wartime politics.

insights.claim: Many in the opposition fear the election was 'not an election but a census': after the war, the judicial overhaul and an aging, apparently corrupt government, the Jewish vote barely moved, which suggests the next election will be worse for them.
insights.speaker: Natan Sachs
insights.so_what: Demographics favor the religious right, so the opposition's window may be closing.
insights.quote: this is in some way not an election but a census

insights.claim: Joel Braunold says the outgoing far-right coalition ran on depopulating the West Bank and Gaza, and its members are already claiming Arab parties 'stole' the election through voter fraud.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Expect claims that the result is illegitimate, which would weigh on post-election stability.

insights.claim: Natan Sachs expects new elections to be the path of least resistance and the 'least unlikely' outcome, with a national unity government as the main alternative; every scenario requires breaking major campaign promises.
insights.speaker: Natan Sachs
insights.so_what: Base case is prolonged caretaker government and a repeat election.
insights.quote: The question is which promise is broken.

insights.claim: Netanyahu is less afraid of a repeat election than the opposition because he ran an inefficient campaign (satellite parties below the threshold, unsigned surplus-vote agreements) and expects to gain seats next round.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Netanyahu's leverage comes from credibly threatening new elections.

insights.claim: The ultra-Orthodox parties may defect from Netanyahu: a unity government would likely leave them out, as happened in 2013 with Lapid and Bennett, so protecting draft exemptions could push them toward the opposition.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Ultra-Orthodox realignment is the wildcard that could break the bloc structure.

insights.claim: Natan Sachs judges the promise easiest to break is the one on ultra-Orthodox conscription, because national-security issues dominate voters and Arab-party cooperation is seen as security-linked.
insights.speaker: Natan Sachs
insights.so_what: A deal trading draft exemptions for power is more likely than an Arab-backed government.

insights.claim: Benjamin Wittes sees no long-term coalition possible except the hard-right religious combination; any alternative government could manage only 3-4 agenda items over about six months before new elections.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes
insights.so_what: Any non-Netanyahu government would be short-lived and narrow in what it can do.
insights.quote: everybody would be thinking in no more than six month increments right now

insights.claim: Natan Sachs argues Netanyahu's goal is to stay prime minister, not merely to stay out of prison, since he turned down plea deals that would have required a 7-year political ban; he would not join a unity government unless he leads it, and while on trial he can only serve as prime minister, not as a minister.
insights.speaker: Natan Sachs
insights.so_what: Any unity government most likely has Netanyahu as prime minister.
insights.quote: His goal is to remain prime minister for as long as he can.

insights.claim: Natan Sachs suggests the opposition might deliberately let Netanyahu take the first mandate so the 28+14-day clock runs against him, although that leaves him in the driver's seat.
insights.speaker: Natan Sachs
insights.so_what: Sequencing of mandates is itself a tactical weapon.

insights.claim: Before a government is sworn in, the Knesset is sovereign: Eisenkot's camp could replace the Speaker and the chairs of the foreign affairs and security, appropriations and arrangements committees, and push an October 7th commission or a 'defendants law' aimed at Netanyahu.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Control of the Knesset security committee could constrain unilateral military action against Iran.

insights.claim: The Jerusalem Post reports Trump wants a unity government without Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, whom Netanyahu has cited as blocking the 20-point plan pushed by Jared Kushner.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: US pressure favors a centrist unity outcome and weakens Netanyahu's threat of new elections.

insights.claim: Joel Braunold predicts that the more Trump gets involved and pushes for unity now, the weaker Netanyahu's bargaining position becomes, because his leverage rests on not fearing another election.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: US involvement is a key variable to watch over the next 45 days.
insights.quote: the more uncomfortable it will be for Prime Minister Netanyahu

insights.claim: European governments and the DNC would prefer an Eisenkot government that relies on the Joint List, because its demands (family reunification, pulling back from Gaza) match the Western consensus and could help Israel avoid planned international sanctions.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: A government's composition could directly affect Israel's exposure to sanctions.

insights.claim: Natan Sachs says Netanyahu sees the remaining two years of the Trump administration as a window to change the reality with Iran before a less favorable US president arrives.
insights.speaker: Natan Sachs
insights.so_what: Raises the risk of renewed Israel-Iran military escalation through 2028.

insights.claim: In his closing campaign interview, Netanyahu declared that US aid to Israel is ending, said Israel must prepare to be a sanctioned economy facing banking sanctions, and suggested using crypto to get around them.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: The sitting PM is openly signaling sanctions risk for Israeli banks and the shekel.
insights.quote: Israel has to prepare to be a sanctioned economy and that banking sanctions are coming

insights.claim: The Bank of Israel responded that crypto-based sanctions evasion is not possible, and Netanyahu replied that they would do as they are told; FDD was shocked and said a high-tech, Nasdaq-linked economy cannot live with bank sanctions.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Friction between the government and the central bank adds to risk for Israeli assets.

insights.claim: High-tech workers, who are portable and drive the Israeli economy, might leave along with their investments if the current coalition is re-elected, and ultra-Orthodox communities that depend on state subsidies and charity would be badly hurt by a sanctions economy.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Sanctions risk could push the ultra-Orthodox to realign and could drive tech capital out of Israel.

insights.claim: Joel Braunold says the region and Washington will not wait through endless election rounds, and nobody wants a kinetic war with Iran fought during another election campaign.
insights.speaker: Joel Braunold
insights.so_what: Outside pressure makes a quicker resolution more likely than in 2019-2022.
